newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak EU exclusion could hit investment - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Slovak EU exclusion could hit investment - analysts.

text.p: Slovakia's exclusion from the first round of European Union enlargement may hit investor confidence and the inflow of foreign capital despite official assurances of business as usual, economists said on Friday.
The European Commission (EC) said on Wednesday that Slovakia's record on political reforms had ruled it out of the first wave of European Union membership talks.

"There is no reason for panic, our work continues unchanged," Economics Ministry spokesman Jozef Sucha told Reuters. "We are still an associate member of the Union and therefore we don't expect any change in our current relations (with the EU)," he added.
But independent analysts said they expected a cooling of private capital's attitude towards Slovakia, although they did not foresee new trade barriers.
"I don't think our access to European markets will suddenly worsen," Juraj Rencko chief economic forecaster at the Academy of Science told Reuters.
Slovakia imports roughly 40 percent from and exports some 45 percent to EU countries.
"What I fear is that a further decrease in the already slow inflow of foreign investment will happen soon," Rencko said.
Cumulative foreign direct investment (FDI) in Slovakia from January 1990 to the end of 1996 totalled $887 million, far below neighbouring Czech Republic, Hungary or Poland.

The largest portion of foreign investment went into industrial production, including projects such as Volkswagen AG's Bratislava car plant, Britain's Tesco Stores and the Slovalco aluminium production joint-venture, involving Norwegian Norsk Hydro's Hydro Aluminium unit.
"(With a drop in FDI) weaker Slovak ratings will probably follow resulting in worse access to loans and resulting in higher debt service costs," Rencko said.

The European Commission relegated Bratislava from the first round of negotiations on EU enlargement due to its bad political record including government disregard for the constitution, the rights of the opposition and the constant tension between the government and the president.
Slovak government officials have accused the Commission of exaggerating minor political problems and have said the exclusion will have no impact.

"This is no catastrophe," Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar said earlier this week. "This is not a final decision only a recommendation and we still have four months in which to prepare for such a decision."
An EU summit in Luxembourg in December is to take a final decision on countries invited to EU enlargement talks.
"If Slovakia fails to join the EU then access to the EU markets will definitely worsen with an immediate impact on the dynamics of the GDP and living standards," Rencko said.

NATO last week invited the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland to join the alliance. The government said NATO had used different criteria to judge Slovakia's suitabilty to those used for other aspirants.
Slovakia was still seen among the frontrunners for both early NATO and EU membership when Czechoslovakia peacefully split into separate states in 1993.

But the U.S. and other western allies have criticised Slovakia for four rocky years of opaque political infighting, problems in dealing with the Hungarian minority, and major shortcomings in media and other reforms.
